cues.text: Let us now work through some additional design and protocol practice, starting with a campus network design question.
Imagine a campus with three buildings.
We want to compare two designs.
The first uses a single shared core.
The second uses two distribution and core switches, connected with redundant fibre uplinks.
The second design costs more, but it reduces single points of failure.
A single point of failure is any one component whose breakdown takes down the whole service.
To strengthen the second design further, use independent power supplies and physically diverse cable routes whenever that is feasible.
Otherwise, one cut trench or one power outage could still defeat the redundancy you paid for.
Next, two terms that people often confuse.
Load balancing spreads requests across healthy servers.
Failover transfers service to another component when the first one becomes unavailable.
They solve different problems.
Then there is backup, which restores lost data.
Be careful here: neither load balancing nor redundant links guarantees data recovery.
If data is deleted or corrupted, a second server or a second cable will not bring it back; only a backup will.
A good design also needs operational discipline.
Define the capacity you will have during a failure, not only when everything is healthy.
Test convergence, meaning how the network settles on new paths after a fault, and test your restore procedures.
And maintain three records: an as-built physical diagram, a logical topology, and a change log.
Now let us review key protocols and port numbers.
A DNS request may use UDP or TCP port 53.
HTTP normally uses TCP port 80.
HTTPS uses TCP port 443, although HTTP/3 uses QUIC over UDP.
SSH uses TCP port 22.
SMTP is commonly TCP port 25 for relay.
DHCP supplies IPv4 configuration using four steps: Discover, Offer, Request, and Acknowledge.
We abbreviate this as DORA.
ICMP supports error reporting and diagnostics.
Remember that a successful ping is not proof that an application is available, because the host may answer ICMP while the web service itself is down.
Finally, a switch's frame forwarding and a router's packet forwarding operate at different scopes.
The switch forwards frames within a local network, while the router forwards packets between networks.
Let us finish with a practice essay.

The task is: explain how each OSI layer contributes to a student loading a portal, and identify where a broken fibre, a wrong VLAN, a missing route, a blocked TCP port, a certificate error, and an HTTP 500 should be investigated.
Here is the model reasoning, in order.
A broken fibre is investigated at the physical layer.
A wrong VLAN is a data-link issue.
A missing route belongs to the network layer.
A blocked TCP port falls under transport and policy.
A certificate error points to the TLS and application stack.
And an HTTP 500 is investigated at the application service.
One last point: troubleshooting layers interact, so always confirm actual evidence rather than assuming the first layer you suspect is the cause.
